This is a recording of a live AI engineering conference in New York about AI agents, finance, and software. Hi. Hey, Dick. Hey, Davis. Hey, Ian. Hi, everyone. Welcome to AI Engineer New York. I'm super excited to be here today. My name is Allie Howe. I'm a member of technical staff at KeyCard. I'm here with some amazing panelists today. We have Ian, CEO of KeyCard. We have Michael Davis, global chief security architect at JPMorgan Chase. And we have Dick Hart, the founder of Aoth and co-creator of OAuth with us on stage today. I'm super excited to talk to all of them about intent-based authorization. And to set the stage, I want to bring to light that as more companies are looking to give their agents increased levels of autonomy, they're looking to runtime authorization to help. Runtime auth is the practice of authorizing an agent per tool call rather than having the agent hold broad standing access that it will eventually misuse. However, is this tool call or not is never a simple question. This is because many MCP tools and APIs are coarse-grained, humans struggle to write the perfect policy, and the environment around the agent will change as it runs. Intent can help by providing extra context so that at runtime, we can make better authorization decisions about what an agent is allowed or is not allowed to do. So to continue, I would like to talk about, really dive into, why do we need intent-based auth in the first place? Models have dramatically improved. They have bigger context windows. They're able to verify work because model vision capabilities have improved. In many contexts, people are proclaiming that AGI is here. If the models are so good, if AGI is really here today, then why are teams struggling to give their agents more autonomy? Ian, let's start with you. You're helping many financial enterprises at KeyCard. What are you seeing that's getting in the way? I think, broadly speaking, enterprises, especially financial services firms, regulated industries, are almost always security first. It's how they build trust in their business and maintaining the business continuity is our first priority. Then innovation is second, third, or fourth. I think, broadly speaking, in any enterprise, what you see is this hodgepodge of different little islands, of different little identities, of different little systems from across all different worlds. How do you actually tie that together in a way that an agent can navigate through that, ask for access, and then also ensure that the agent cannot perform something that was unintended by the user or the business? The unfortunate situation is most of our systems today are coarse-grained. I don't know if Salesforce is a good example. For a very long time, they had a single scope, which was API on their OAuth, which is, in the context of an agent, not very helpful. That's, broadly, the first and foremost part, is that most of the systems they have for security today were designed for a world where humans were making all the decisions and software was very deterministic, not this newfangled magic box we've invented that basically reasons and tries over and over again to find a solution to a problem. Doug, how is OAuth part of the problem? How is OAuth getting in the way, and why is it not the right fit for agents? When people started looking at how do we authorize agents to access something, the tool that was sitting there on the shelf was OAuth. People grabbed that tool and said, here's a tool. This is authorization. It should be able to solve the problem. But OAuth was not designed for this kind of world. It was designed originally for how do I let this website talk to this website? In OAuth 2, we added scopes. Before that, it was just do anything. But it required you to be preregistered. It's expecting that there's a browser involved in a redirect. OAuth has evolved over the years to support some other things. But the agent-centric world is completely different. We don't know ahead of time what the agent needs to do. We need to go and make that decision over time. Different instances of an agent are going to need different kinds of things. And as Ian talked about, the granularity of the scopes that people says, well, we already have scopes for OAuth. Let's just map those over to agents is far too coarse-grained for what agents are doing. Davis, how are you seeing enterprises move towards higher levels of autonomy? I think the key piece is how do you deal with that coarse-grained problem? And what I've seen in the more successful enterprises is they kind of board agents like they onboard developers. You don't get full commit access day one. You're actually having to go through and add the levels of capability as they mature. And so the definitions that enterprises are coming up with, what is the context that makes this agent safe? And it isn't just usually what the agent says. It can attest to something, but it's other things like the environment around it and other information that can help you understand levels of autonomy. A very simple example would be where is the sandbox running? Is it in the sandbox? Those type of things can change the level of autonomy that's allowed. Absolutely. As we mentioned that coarse-grained access problem, and to put that into perspective, to give an example, with Notion's MCP server, you can say fetch this page, which is like the view page tool or get page, but you can't say just get this database on this page. How is runtime authorization based on intent a better model? That's for anyone. I'll take a shot at it. So to me, this is something that the financial services industry, hopefully maybe we can learn from the background that banks have gone through. Banks moved long ago from authorizing and authenticating humans to authorizing the transaction. And when is that transaction occurring? At runtime. And so I think that runtime authorization is we're going to be able to learn from the scars of the past that we've had and apply it to this new problem. I also think that one thing is it's a lot easier to debug something at runtime when you understand the intent. We all remember back in the day writing checks or seeing those things on TV now, I guess is the right thing. But writing checks, there was a memo field there. That memo field was used to actually tell the intent of what this payment was. But the check itself did have limits, the price, the payee, the date, et cetera. I think a lot of those concepts are now being applied and can be applied to help with this runtime. Intent is sort of one of those, like many words, words are hard. And so building on the example here of making a payment of a transaction, that's not a scope. That's can I do this one thing in this particular context? Well, this one payment. But I think we need an agent. To make a decision, should it be able to do it, you need all the rest of the context of, well, why are we making this payment?
